At each decode step, the model produces a vector of raw scores — one per token in the vocabulary — called logits. A vocabulary of 100,000 tokens produces 100,000 logit values. These scores are then converted to probabilities via a softmax operation, which exponentiates each value and normalises the result so all probabilities sum to 1.
...
The sampling strategy then decides which token from this distribution to select. This is where temperature, top-k, and top-p come in — they each modify either the distribution itself or the subset from which selection is made.
...
For a factual prompt like this, the distribution is sharply peaked. Temperature, top-k, and top-p all behave differently on peaked vs. flat distributions.

The simplest strategy: always pick the token with the highest probability. No randomness, no parameters to tune. The output is fully deterministic — the same prompt will always produce exactly the same output.

Temperature is a scalar applied to the logits before the softmax. Dividing logits by a value greater than 1 flattens the distribution — high-probability tokens become less dominant, low-probability tokens become more plausible. Dividing by a value less than 1 sharpens the distribution — the highest-probability token gets even more probability mass concentrated on it.
...
High temperature doesn't mean random — it means the long tail of the distribution has more influence. At very high temperatures, low-quality tokens become sampled often enough to degrade coherence.
...
A temperature of 1.0 means the softmax is applied to the raw logits unchanged. This is the baseline the model was trained with. Values below 1.0 make the model more confident and consistent; values above 1.0 increase entropy and diversity.
...
## Top-k sampling
...
Top-k restricts sampling to the k highest-probability tokens, then re-normalises and samples from that subset. If k=50, the model considers only the 50 most likely next tokens — regardless of how much of the probability mass they collectively represent.
...
The problem with a fixed k is that it's context-insensitive. On a peaked distribution (one token at 95%), k=50 includes 49 essentially irrelevant tokens. On a flat distribution (50 tokens each at 2%), k=50 captures the entire meaningful distribution. The same k value behaves very differently depending on the shape of the logits.
...
## Top-p (nucleus) sampling
...
Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, is designed to address this. Instead of a fixed count of tokens, top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p. If p=0.9, the model samples from however many tokens it takes to cover 90% of the probability mass.
...
On a peaked distribution, the nucleus might be just 3–5 tokens. On a flat distribution, it might be 500. The vocabulary size adapts to the shape of each individual prediction, which is why nucleus sampling tends to produce more coherent text than top-k across a wide range of prompts.
...
// Top-p + temperature together
...
Most production systems apply temperature first (reshaping the distribution), then top-p (selecting the nucleus), then sample. The order matters — temperature applied before top-p means the nucleus size changes with temperature. Applying them in different orders produces different results, though frameworks generally handle this consistently.

Author: N/A
Highlights:
Most engineers treat LLM quality regressions as a prompt engineering problem or a model capability problem. They rewrite system prompts, try a newer model, or add few-shot examples. They rarely check the three numbers sitting silently at the top of every API call: temperature, top-p, and top-k. But those defaults are shape-shifting every response your model produces, and tuning them wrong causes output variance that teams blame on the model for months before realizing the culprit was a configuration value they never touched.
...
Temperature, top-p, and top-k each operate at a different point in the same sampling pipeline: raw logits come out of the model, get filtered and reshaped, and then a token is drawn from the resulting probability distribution.
...
Temperature scales the logits before converting them to probabilities via softmax:`P(token) = softmax(logits / temperature)`. A value below 1.0 sharpens the distribution—likely tokens become more likely, unlikely tokens become nearly impossible. A value above 1.0 flattens it—probabilities become more uniform, and the model explores a broader vocabulary. Temperature controls how peaked vs. diffuse the distribution is.
...
Top-p (nucleus sampling) works after temperature is applied. It sorts tokens by probability, walks down the ranked list, and keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches the threshold p. Everything else is discarded. If p=0.95, you're sampling from whichever tokens collectively account for 95% of the probability mass. The key behavior: when the model is confident, the nucleus is small (a few tokens cover 95%). When it's uncertain, the nucleus expands (many tokens share probability mass).
...
Top-k is simpler and less adaptive: keep exactly the k highest-probability tokens, regardless of their actual probabilities. If k=50, you always sample from 50 candidates. The limitation is that a flat distribution at rank 50 still gets included even if it represents noise.
...
Repetition/frequency/presence penalties are applied before the truncation step. Repetition penalty divides logit values for previously-seen tokens (multiplying by 1/penalty). Frequency penalty subtracts proportionally to how often a token has appeared. Presence penalty applies a flat deduction to any token that appeared at all. The penalty type matters more than the value: presence penalty is aggressive and binary (saw it once = penalized forever), which breaks natural language that depends on pronouns, articles, and common words.
...
The belief that setting temperature=0 produces repeatable, stable outputs is one of the most expensive misconceptions in production AI. Temperature=0 means greedy decoding: always select the single highest-probability token. But in a real inference environment, the "highest-probability token" is not a stable quantity.
...
The most common tuning mistake happens when engineers want "more creative" outputs and adjust both parameters simultaneously. The reasoning is intuitive: temperature controls creativity, top-p controls diversity, raising both should produce diverse and creative output. The actual result is often incoherent garbage.
...
Here's why. When temperature increases from 0.5 to 1.5, the probability distribution flattens. At temperature=0.5, your top token might have 80% probability—top-p=0.95 only needs a handful of tokens to reach that threshold. At temperature=1.5, the same model might assign 35% to the top token—top-p=0.95 now requires dozens of tokens to accumulate to 95%, including low-quality candidates that would have been discarded at lower temperatures. Raising temperature expands the nucleus automatically, even if you don't touch top-p.
...
The general rule: treat temperature and top-p as coupled, not independent. If you raise temperature, lower top-p. If you raise top-p, consider lowering temperature. Changing both in the same direction amplifies their interaction in ways that are hard to predict without testing.

Instead of a fixed cumulative probability, min-p keeps tokens whose probability exceeds a fraction of the peak token's probability. When the model is confident (peak=0.95), the threshold scales up automatically. When it's uncertain (peak=0.1), the threshold scales down. ...

Curate 100-500 examples that cover your actual input distribution—including edge cases, ambiguous inputs, and adversarial examples that exercise the failure modes you care about. ...
A logit can be any real number, positive or negative, and on its own it is not a probability. The`softmax` converts the whole set of logits into probabilities by exponentiating each one and dividing by the sum of all the exponentials, which guarantees every value lands between 0 and 1 and the set sums to exactly 1. That exponential step is why the gap between a high logit and a low one matters so much, and it is precisely the quantity temperature rescales in the next section. Greedy decoding ignores the shape of the distribution entirely and keeps only the argmax, which is why every decision about what to do with the rest of the mass belongs to sampling.
...
Temperature scales the logits by dividing them before the softmax is applied (Hinton et al., 2015). A low temperature sharpens the distribution, so the top token's lead grows and output becomes more deterministic and focused. A high temperature flattens it, so long-shot tokens get more of a chance and output becomes more diverse and surprising. At the limit, temperature → 0 is exactly greedy decoding: the argmax token wins every time. By convention`T = 1` leaves the model's raw distribution unchanged. Crucially, temperature reshapes how probable each token is, acting on a different axis from the truncation knobs you'll meet next.
...
Even after temperature, the model still assigns a tiny probability to thousands of nonsense tokens. Sampling from that whole "long tail" is what produces gibberish. Truncation fixes this by throwing the tail away before you sample. Top-k sampling keeps only the k highest-probability tokens, renormalizes over them, and samples from that fixed-size set (Fan et al., 2018). Top-p sampling (also called nucleus sampling) instead keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, then renormalizes over that "nucleus" (Holtzman et al., 2019). The key difference: top-k fixes the count of candidates, while top-p fixes the probability mass, so the number of candidates in top-p adapts to each step, staying small when the model is confident and widening when it's unsure.

Role-play prompting is known to steer the behavior of language models by injecting a persona into the prompt, improving their zero-shot reasoning capabilities. However, such improvements are inconsistent across different tasks or instances. This inconsistency suggests that zero-shot and role-play prompting may offer complementary strengths rather than one being universally superior. Building on this insight, we propose **Persona Switch**, a novel decoding method that dynamically combines the benefits of both prompting strategies. Our method proceeds step-by-step, selecting the better output between zero-shot and role-play prompting at each step by comparing their output confidence, as measured by the logit gap. Most engineers treat LLM quality regressions as a prompt engineering problem or a model capability problem. They rewrite system prompts, try a newer model, or add few-shot examples. They rarely check the three numbers sitting silently at the top of every API call: temperature, top-p, and top-k. But those defaults are shape-shifting every response your model produces, and tuning them wrong causes output variance that teams blame on the model for months before realizing the culprit was a configuration value they never touched.

![](https://opengraph-image.blockeden.xyz/api/og-tianpan-co?title=Sampling%20Parameters%20in%20Production%3A%20The%20Tuning%20Decisions%20Nobody%20Explains)

This isn't an introductory explainer. If you're running LLMs in production—for extraction pipelines, code generation, summarization, or any output that feeds into real systems—these are the mechanics and tradeoffs you need to understand before you can tune intelligently.

## What These Parameters Actually Do[​](#what-these-parameters-actually-do "Direct link to What These Parameters Actually Do")

Temperature, top-p, and top-k each operate at a different point in the same sampling pipeline: raw logits come out of the model, get filtered and reshaped, and then a token is drawn from the resulting probability distribution.

**Temperature** scales the logits before converting them to probabilities via softmax: `P(token) = softmax(logits / temperature)`. A value below 1.0 sharpens the distribution—likely tokens become more likely, unlikely tokens become nearly impossible. A value above 1.0 flattens it—probabilities become more uniform, and the model explores a broader vocabulary. Temperature controls how peaked vs. diffuse the distribution is.

**Top-p (nucleus sampling)** works after temperature is applied. It sorts tokens by probability, walks down the ranked list, and keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches the threshold p. Everything else is discarded. If p=0.95, you're sampling from whichever tokens collectively account for 95% of the probability mass. The key behavior: when the model is confident, the nucleus is small (a few tokens cover 95%). When it's uncertain, the nucleus expands (many tokens share probability mass).

**Top-k** is simpler and less adaptive: keep exactly the k highest-probability tokens, regardless of their actual probabilities. If k=50, you always sample from 50 candidates. The limitation is that a flat distribution at rank 50 still gets included even if it represents noise.

# Sampling & Decoding

Temperature, Top-p, Top-k, and How Outputs Are Actually Chosen

After the model computes a probability distribution over its vocabulary, something has to pick the next token. That decision — made thousands of times per response — determines whether the output is creative or conservative, coherent or chaotic. These are the mechanics behind that choice.

20 min read

## From logits to tokens

At each decode step, the model produces a vector of raw scores — one per token in the vocabulary — called **logits**. A vocabulary of 100,000 tokens produces 100,000 logit values. These scores are then converted to probabilities via a softmax operation, which exponentiates each value and normalises the result so all probabilities sum to 1.

The sampling strategy then decides which token from this distribution to select. This is where temperature, top-k, and top-p come in — they each modify either the distribution itself or the subset from which selection is made.

// decode step — logits to token

Prompt: "The capital of France is" — top candidates after softmax

"Paris"0.82

"Lyon"0.08

"Nice"0.04

"Bordeaux"0.02

... 99,996 more0.04

For a factual prompt like this, the distribution is sharply peaked. Temperature, top-k, and top-p all behave differently on peaked vs. flat distributions.

## Greedy decoding

The simplest strategy: always pick the token with the highest probability. No randomness, no parameters to tune. The output is fully deterministic — the same prompt will always produce exactly the same output.

Greedy decoding works well for tasks where the correct answer is unambiguous and you want reproducibility: classification, structured extraction, code generation in narrow domains. It fails on longer or more open-ended generations because it gets stuck in repetitive loops — once a locally high-probability token is chosen, it can set up conditions where the same token stays highest on subsequent steps.

## Temperature

Temperature is a scalar applied to the logits _before_ the softmax. Dividing logits by a value greater than 1 flattens the distribution — high-probability tokens become less dominant, low-probability tokens become more plausible. Dividing by a value less than 1 sharpens the distribution — the highest-probability token gets even more probability mass concentrated on it.

// temperature effect on distribution

Same logits, different temperatures — "Paris" probability:

temp = 0.1≈0.99 — near greedy

temp = 1.00.82 — default

temp = 1.5≈0.55 — more varied

temp = 2.0≈0.30 — high entropy

High temperature doesn't mean random — it means the long tail of the distribution has more influence. At very high temperatures, low-quality tokens become sampled often enough to degrade coherence.

A temperature of 1.0 means the softmax is applied to the raw logits unchanged. This is the baseline the model was trained with. Values below 1.0 make the model more confident and consistent; values above 1.0 increase entropy and diversity.

// Temperature = 0 is not greedy decoding

Setting temperature to 0 is mathematically undefined (dividing by zero), but most frameworks interpret it as greedy decoding — argmax over the logits. In practice, "temperature 0" and "greedy" are equivalent in every inference framework you're likely to use, but they're conceptually distinct operations.

## Top-k sampling

Top-k restricts sampling to the k highest-probability tokens, then re-normalises and samples from that subset. If k=50, the model considers only the 50 most likely next tokens — regardless of how much of the probability mass they collectively represent.

The problem with a fixed k is that it's context-insensitive. On a peaked distribution (one token at 95%), k=50 includes 49 essentially irrelevant tokens. On a flat distribution (50 tokens each at 2%), k=50 captures the entire meaningful distribution. The same k value behaves very differently depending on the shape of the logits.

## Top-p (nucleus) sampling

Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, is designed to address this. Instead of a fixed count of tokens, top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p. If p=0.9, the model samples from however many tokens it takes to cover 90% of the probability mass.

On a peaked distribution, the nucleus might be just 3–5 tokens. On a flat distribution, it might be 500\. The vocabulary size adapts to the shape of each individual prediction, which is why nucleus sampling tends to produce more coherent text than top-k across a wide range of prompts.

// Top-p + temperature together

Most production systems apply temperature first (reshaping the distribution), then top-p (selecting the nucleus), then sample. The order matters — temperature applied before top-p means the nucleus size changes with temperature. Applying them in different orders produces different results, though frameworks generally handle this consistently.

## Beam search

All of the above are sample-once-and-move-on strategies. Beam search is different: it maintains multiple candidate sequences simultaneously, extending each one at every step and pruning the worst candidates. With a beam width of 4, you track the 4 highest-probability partial sequences and evaluate them in parallel.

# F5: Creative freedom

## Summary

Temperature, top-p, and top-k form a coupled pipeline that controls how much creative variance an LLM exhibits — production best practice is to tune temperature deliberately, leave top-p at provider defaults, and ignore top-k entirely. Branching techniques (Tree of Thoughts, DPWriter, MCTS) enable systematic exploration of multiple creative trajectories at inference time by expanding and pruning trees of candidate continuations. Persona switching is formalised as a pattern language with dynamic transitions, used in production for multi-role agents and interactive fiction. Agentic exploration loops (APEX, ReTreVal) solve the "exploration collapse" problem by maintaining explicit strategy maps and reflexion memory buffers that compound learning across episodes. Together these techniques form a spectrum from fine-grained token-level control (temperature/p) to macro-level creative search (branching, persona shifts, exploration loops), each with distinct production deployment patterns.

## Findings

### [1] Temperature reshapes the logit distribution before softmax — values below 1.0 sharpen (more deterministic), above 1.0 flatten (more creative) — and is the primary production knob for creative control.
- quote: "Temperature scales the logits before converting them to probabilities via softmax: `P(token) = softmax(logits / temperature)`. A value below 1.0 sharpens the distribution... A value above 1.0 flattens it—probabilities become more uniform, and the model explores a broader vocabulary."
- url: https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-04-18-sampling-parameters-production-temperature-top-p-tuning
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026-04-18
- confidence: high

### [2] Top-p (nucleus sampling) adaptively truncates to the smallest token set whose cumulative probability exceeds threshold p — it is strictly preferred over top-k in production because it adapts to distribution shape per-step.
- quote: "Top-p, also called nucleus sampling, is designed to address this [context-insensitivity]. Instead of a fixed count of tokens, top-p keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p... On a peaked distribution, the nucleus might be just 3–5 tokens. On a flat distribution, it might be 500."
- url: https://inference-engineering.com/guide-sampling-decoding.html
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026
- confidence: high

### [3] Raising both temperature AND top-p simultaneously is the most common production mistake — they are coupled, and moving both in the same direction amplifies incoherence.
- quote: "The most common tuning mistake happens when engineers want 'more creative' outputs and adjust both parameters simultaneously... When temperature increases from 0.5 to 1.5, the probability distribution flattens... top-p=0.95 now requires dozens of tokens to accumulate to 95%, including low-quality candidates that would have been discarded at lower temperatures."
- url: https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-04-18-sampling-parameters-production-temperature-top-p-tuning
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026-04-18
- confidence: high

### [4] Temperature=0 does NOT guarantee deterministic output in production — GPU floating-point non-associativity, continuous batching, and KV-cache optimisation introduce irreducible variance.
- quote: "The belief that setting temperature=0 produces repeatable, stable outputs is one of the most expensive misconceptions in production AI... Modern inference servers use continuous batching to maximize throughput. Requests that arrive at the same time get batched together, and batch composition affects computation."
- url: https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-04-18-sampling-parameters-production-temperature-top-p-tuning
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026-04-18
- confidence: high

### [5] Min-p sampling (Nguyen et al., ICLR 2025) addresses the flat-distribution problem by making the threshold relative to the model's own peak-token confidence — adopted in vLLM, not yet universal in commercial APIs.
- quote: "Min-p sampling... keeps tokens whose probability exceeds a fraction of the peak token's probability. When the model is confident (peak=0.95), the threshold scales up automatically. When it's uncertain (peak=0.1), the threshold scales down."
- url: https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-04-18-sampling-parameters-production-temperature-top-p-tuning
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026-04-18
- confidence: high

### [6] Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., NeurIPS 2023) enables deliberate creative exploration by maintaining a tree of coherent language-thoughts with BFS/DFS search, self-evaluation, and backtracking — achieving 74% vs 4% on Game of 24 compared to chain-of-thought.
- quote: "ToT allows LMs to perform deliberate decision making by considering multiple different reasoning paths and self-evaluating choices to decide the next course of action, as well as looking ahead or backtracking when necessary to make global choices."
- url: https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2023/file/271db9922b8d1f4dd7aaef84ed5ac703-Paper-Conference.pdf
- source_type: primary
- published: 2023
- confidence: high

### [7] DPWriter (ACL 2026 Oral) introduces Diverse Planning Branching that strategically forks at planning segments in a semi-structured CoT, using n-gram and semantic diversity metrics to select the most divergent trajectories — production deployment for RL-based creative writing with diversity rewards.
- quote: "We introduce a Diverse Planning Branching method that strategically introduces divergence at the planning phase based on diversity variation, alongside a group-aware diversity reward to encourage distinct trajectories."
- url: https://github.com/Aman-4-Real/DPWriter
- source_type: secondary
- published: 2026
- confidence: high

### [8] Persona Switching is formalised as a pattern language (Schmidt, 2024) with Dynamic Persona Switching enabling seamless role transitions within a single session based on contextual triggers — used in production for multi-agent AI workflows, customer support, and interactive fiction.
- quote: "Dynamic Persona Switching enables seamless transitions between personas in response to evolving task requirements... Contextual triggers establish triggers within the task context that indicate when a persona switch is needed based on the evolving context of the task."
- url: https://www.cs.wm.edu/~dcschmidt/PDF/schreiber-PLoP24.pdf
- source_type: primary
- published: 2024
- confidence: high

### [9] APEX (Autonomous Policy Exploration, 2026) solves exploration collapse in self-evolving agents by maintaining an explicit strategy map (a DAG of milestones with prerequisite edges) with Fork Discovery that mines past episodes for unexplored directions and Policy Selection that balances exploration vs exploitation — evaluated on Jericho text-adventure games and WebArena.
- quote: "Self-evolving agents often suffer from exploration collapse: as memory grows, behavior concentrates around familiar high-reward routines, reducing the chance of discovering better alternatives... APEX addresses the root cause: without an explicit strategy space, agents have no way to know what they have not tried."
- url: https://arxiv.org/html/2605.21240
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026-05-20
- confidence: high

### [10] ReTreVal (Reasoning Tree with Validation, 2026) combines Tree-of-Thoughts exploration with node-level self-refinement and a persistent reflexion memory buffer that stores successful reasoning patterns and failure modes across problems — enabling cross-episode learning without fine-tuning.
- quote: "ReTreVal constructs a structured reasoning tree... where each node undergoes iterative self-critique and refinement guided by explicit LLM-generated feedback. A reflexion memory buffer persistently stores insights from successful reasoning paths and failure patterns, enabling cross-problem learning."
- url: https://arxiv.org/html/2601.02880v1
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026
- confidence: high

### [11] Narrative Studio (Ghaffari & Hokamp, 2025) applies Monte Carlo Tree Search to automatically expand promising narrative branches in interactive storytelling, with configurable scoring, look-ahead rollouts, and early stopping — demonstrating MCTS for creative branching in production-like narrative environments.
- quote: "We employ Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to autonomously expand promising story branches, guided by a scoring prompt that rates newly generated events. By iterating through repeated cycles of selection, expansion, simulation, and backpropagation, MCTS discovers high-value narrative paths without relying on exhaustive search."
- url: https://arxiv.org/html/2504.02426
- source_type: primary
- published: 2025-04-03
- confidence: high

### [12] Production guidelines for creative freedom are domain-specific: code generation uses temperature 0.2-0.5 with repetition penalty at 1.0; conversational chat uses 0.3-0.7; creative writing and brainstorming use 0.7-1.0; values above 1.0 are rare and used only to force diversity in batch generation.
- quote: "Code generation: Use temperature 0.2-0.5. Code requires syntax precision, but full greedy decoding can miss valid solutions... Creative writing, brainstorming, generating multiple ideas: 0.7-1.0... > 1.0: Rare in production. Sometimes used to force diversity in batch generation."
- url: https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-04-18-sampling-parameters-production-temperature-top-p-tuning
- source_type: primary
- published: 2026-04-18
- confidence: high
